lessons.title: Combining Metal with Wood, Glass, and Stone
lessons.body:
When you combine metal with wood, glass, or stone, you must think about how they will move and react together. Wood expands and shrinks with humidity, so drill holes in the metal 2mm larger than the bolt diameter to allow for movement. Use stainless steel bolts or galvanized screws to avoid rust stains on wood. For a strong joint, apply a polyurethane adhesive like Sikaflex 11FC between the metal and wood before bolting. In Africa, hardwoods like mukwa, teak, or mahogany work well, but seal them with linseed oil to prevent cracking.

Glass is fragile and can shatter from thermal expansion. When attaching glass to metal, use silicone adhesive (e.g., Dow Corning 795) and avoid drilling holes in the glass unless you have a diamond bit and water cooling. For small glass pieces, embed them in a metal frame with rubber gaskets. Remember that metal conducts heat faster than glass, so in direct sun, the metal can expand and crack the glass. Keep glass pieces under 30cm x 30cm for safety.

Stone is heavy and brittle. Use a diamond-tipped drill and water to make holes in stone. For joining stone to metal, use a two-part epoxy like Pratley Steel or Araldite. Roughen the stone surface with a chisel and clean with acetone before applying epoxy. For outdoor sculptures, avoid limestone as it reacts with acid rain. Granite or basalt is better. Always support the stone from underneath with a metal bracket to prevent it from falling.

When mixing three materials, design the sculpture so each material can expand independently. Use slotted holes or flexible adhesives. In rural areas, you can source wood from local carpenters, glass from broken bottles (melted in a kiln if available), and stone from riverbeds. Test your joints with a hammer tapâa dull sound means a loose bond. Always wear safety glasses and gloves when cutting or drilling these materials.

lessons.title: Found Object Sculpture
lessons.body:
Found object sculpture means using discarded itemsâcar parts, gears, spoons, bicycle chains, nuts, bolts, and scrap metalâto create art. Start by collecting materials from scrapyards, mechanic workshops, or dumpsites. In Africa, you can find rich sources at 'juakali' artisan clusters or metal recycling yards. Look for objects with interesting shapes: old spark plugs, brake discs, machete blades, pots, and wire. Clean them with a wire brush and degreaser (e.g., paraffin or caustic soda) to remove rust and oil.

Before welding or bolting, arrange your objects on a flat surface to plan the composition. Use a chalk or soapstone marker to outline your design. For joining, you can weld (MIG or arc), braze, or use bolts and rivets. If you don't have a welder, use a drill and bolts (M6 or M8) or epoxy. For small pieces, a 2mm drill bit and pop rivets work well. Always test the strength by hanging the sculpture and gently shaking it.

Balance is critical. A top-heavy sculpture will fall. Weigh your materialsâa car gearbox can be 50kg, while a spoon is 20g. Use a scale (even a bathroom scale) to check. Weld a heavy base plate (at least 5mm thick) or fill a metal pipe with concrete for stability. For outdoor pieces, weld all joints fully to prevent water entry. If using dissimilar metals (e.g., aluminium and steel), insulate with a rubber gasket to prevent galvanic corrosion.

Finishing: You can leave the found objects with their original patina or paint them with rust-resistant primer and enamel. For a shiny look, buff with a wire wheel and coat with clear lacquer. Remember that found objects tell a storyâa bicycle chain might represent movement, a hoe blade might represent agriculture. Let the materials guide your theme. Always wear a respirator when grinding or welding, and keep a fire extinguisher nearby.

lessons.title: Adhesives and Bonding Agents for Mixed Media
lessons.body:
Not all adhesives work for metal mixed media. You need to match the adhesive to the materials and the stress. For metal-to-metal, use epoxy (e.g., Pratley Steel, Araldite) or anaerobic adhesives like Loctite 638. For metal-to-wood, polyurethane glue (e.g., Gorilla Glue) or construction adhesive (e.g., Sikaflex 11FC) is best because it flexes with wood movement. For metal-to-glass, use silicone (e.g., Dow Corning 795) or UV-curing adhesive. For metal-to-stone, two-part epoxy is ideal.

Surface preparation is 80% of bond strength. Clean all surfaces with acetone or alcohol to remove oil and dust. Roughen smooth metal with 80-grit sandpaper or a grinder. For glass, clean with vinegar and water. For stone, wire-brush and dry. Mix epoxy exactly as per instructionsâusually 1:1 or 2:1 ratio by volume. Stir for 2 minutes, then apply a thin layer (1-2mm) to both surfaces. Clamp or tape the joint and let it cure for 24 hours at 25Â°C. In cold weather, cure time doubles.

For high-stress joints, combine adhesive with mechanical fasteners. For example, bolt and glue a metal bracket to a wooden base. Use a rivet or screw as a backup. Avoid using hot glue for outdoor sculpturesâit melts at 60Â°C and fails in African sun. Also avoid contact adhesive (e.g., Bostik) for structural joints because it creeps under load. For filling gaps, use epoxy putty (e.g., Pratley Putty) which can be drilled and sanded.

Safety: Work in a ventilated area. Wear nitrile gloves and safety glasses. Epoxy can cause skin irritation. Store adhesives in a cool, dry placeâheat shortens shelf life. In rural areas, you can make a simple adhesive from cassava starch and water for paper or light wood, but it is not waterproof. For permanent outdoor bonds, stick to marine-grade epoxy or polyurethane. Always test a small sample joint before applying to your sculpture.

lessons.title: Mounting and Display Techniques
lessons.body:
How you mount a sculpture affects its stability and how viewers see it. For indoor display, use a base of wood, stone, or metal. The base should be at least 1/3 of the sculpture's height and wider than the sculpture's footprint. For a 1m tall sculpture, a base of 30cm x 30cm and 5cm thick is good. Drill holes in the base and sculpture, then bolt with M8 or M10 bolts. Use a threaded insert in wood to avoid stripping. For heavy pieces, add a metal L-bracket at the back.

For outdoor display, you need a foundation. Dig a hole 30cm deep and 20cm wide. Fill with concrete (1 part cement, 2 parts sand, 3 parts gravel). Embed a metal rod or pipe (at least 12mm diameter) in the concrete and weld or bolt your sculpture to it. Make sure the sculpture is at least 10cm above ground to prevent water pooling. For large pieces, use a plinth of stone or concrete. In public spaces, consider securityâweld a chain to the base and lock it to a ground anchor.

Wall-mounted sculptures need a French cleat or a metal bracket. Attach a 45-degree beveled piece of wood or metal to the wall and a matching piece to the sculpture. Use wall anchors (e.g., Fischer Duopower) rated for at least 2 times the sculpture's weight. For heavy pieces, use a metal Z-clip. Always check that the wall is solidâavoid drywall or weak plaster. In museums, they use adjustable mounts with brass rods, but for your workshop, simple L-brackets work.

Lighting: Position your sculpture so light hits it from the side to show texture. For outdoor, consider the sun's pathâin Africa, the sun is strong, so use a matte finish to reduce glare. For indoor, a spotlight from below or above can create drama. Rotate your sculpture occasionally to check all angles. Finally, label your work with a small metal plate or engraved tag showing your name, title, and year. This adds professionalism and helps buyers.

lessons.title: Weatherproofing Outdoor Sculptures
lessons.body:
Outdoor sculptures in Africa face intense sun, rain, dust, and temperature swings. To protect them, you must seal every joint and surface. Start with a rust-resistant primer. For steel, use a zinc-rich primer (e.g., Rust-Oleum 7769) or red oxide primer. Apply two coats with a brush or spray, letting each dry for 4 hours. For aluminium, use a self-etching primer. For galvanized metal, clean with vinegar and apply a galvanized primer. Then topcoat with a UV-resistant enamel or polyurethane paint (e.g., Dulux Gloss). Avoid cheap lacquersâthey peel within months.

For wood, seal with a marine varnish or linseed oil. Apply three coats, sanding lightly between coats. For thatch or rope, treat with a borate solution to prevent rot and insects. For stone, apply a silicone sealer (e.g., Lithofin) to make it water-repellent. For glass, ensure it is tempered or laminated; if not, cover with a clear UV film. All adhesives must be marine-grade. If you used epoxy, check for cracks and reapply as needed.

Drainage is critical. Drill a 5mm hole at the lowest point of any hollow metal part to let water out. For bases, angle them slightly so water runs off. Avoid creating pockets where water can sit. For moving parts, use stainless steel bearings or bushings, and grease them with waterproof grease (e.g., lithium grease). In coastal areas, salt accelerates corrosionâwash your sculpture with fresh water every month and reapply wax (e.g., carnauba wax) to metal surfaces.

Inspection: Check your sculpture every 3 months. Look for rust spots, loose bolts, and cracked paint. Touch up with a small brush. If you live in a region with acid rain (e.g., near industrial areas), use a polyurethane clear coat. For extreme sun, consider a shade structure or plant a tree nearby. Remember that weathering can add characterâsome artists let rust form a patina. But if you want longevity, maintenance is key. Keep a log of treatments and dates.

lessons.title: Project: Mixed Media Assemblage
lessons.body:
For this project, you will create a mixed media assemblage that combines metal with at least two other materials (wood, glass, or stone) and includes one found object. The sculpture should be at least 40cm tall and stable. Start by sketching your idea. Choose a themeâe.g., 'Harvest' using a hoe blade, wood, and glass beads, or 'Urban Life' using car parts, stone, and wire. Gather materials: a metal base (e.g., a brake disc or steel plate), wood offcuts, broken glass (tumbled smooth), and a found object like a spoon or gear.

Step 1: Prepare materials. Clean metal with wire brush and degreaser. Cut wood to size and sand smooth. For glass, if using broken bottles, tumble in a rock tumbler with sand and water for 24 hours to remove sharp edges. For stone, select a flat piece and clean. Step 2: Build the armature. Weld or bolt a metal rod (6mm) to the base. This will support the other elements. Step 3: Attach wood. Drill holes and bolt wood to the metal rod using M6 bolts and epoxy. Step 4: Attach glass. Use silicone adhesive to glue glass pieces to the wood or metal. Let cure for 24 hours. Step 5: Attach found object. Weld or bolt the found object to the metal. If welding, protect nearby wood with a wet cloth.

Step 6: Finish. Paint metal with primer and enamel. Seal wood with varnish. Polish glass with a soft cloth. Step 7: Mount. Attach the sculpture to a wooden or stone base with bolts. Ensure it stands level. Step 8: Document. Take photos from all sides and write a short description of your materials and meaning. Present your work to the class or post online with #riseAFRICAsculpture.

Safety: Wear gloves, safety glasses, and a respirator when cutting, grinding, or welding. Work in a well-ventilated area. Keep a first aid kit nearby. Time: This project should take 8-10 hours over 2-3 days. Cost: Aim to spend under $20 by using scrap materials. If you sell it, price at least 3 times material cost plus labor. This project will test your joining, balancing, and finishing skills.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Mixed Media and Assemblage in African Metal Sculpture

Mixed media and assemblage sculpture is where African metal artists turn scrap, offcuts, and found materials into sellable high-value work. In workshops from Dakar to Harare, the economics are simple: steel gives structure and volume, wood adds warmth and cultural narrative, glass and stone add perceived value, and found objects add story. Buyers pay for story. This practical reference gives you the working knowledge to combine materials safely, bond them permanently, mount them professionally, and weatherproof them for outdoor commissions â the four skills that separate a hobbyist from a studio that wins contracts.

1. Combining Metal with Wood, Glass, and Stone

Every material you add to steel brings a different expansion rate, weight, and failure mode. The table below is your buying and design reference. In African workshops, hardwood offcuts (iroko, mahogany, mukwa, mvule) and local stone (granite, soapstone, laterite) are usually cheaper than imported fixings, so design around what is available locally.

Table 1: Material pairing guide for mixed media sculpture
Material Typical expansion (per Â°C) Best fixing method Main risk
Mild steel ~12 Âµm/m Welding, bolting Rust staining adjacent materials
Hardwood (iroko, mukwa) ~40â60 Âµm/m (across grain) Slotted holes, isolation tape Cracking; moisture swelling
Glass (annealed) ~9 Âµm/m Silicone + mechanical clip Thermal shock, edge impact
Stone (granite/soapstone) ~8â12 Âµm/m Anchor bolts, epoxy pins Weight; brittle under point load

Source: expansion coefficients compiled from Engineering ToolBox, "Coefficients of Linear Thermal Expansion" (engineeringtoolbox.com), and conservation data in the Canadian Conservation Institute's "Agents of Deterioration" resource (canada.ca).

2. Found Object Sculpture

Found object work is the highest-margin line in most African metal studios because material cost is near zero. Sources worth cultivating: scrapyards, panel beaters, borehole and pump repair shops, bottling plants (crown caps, wire cages), and market traders discarding tin. Build a supply relationship, not a one-off visit â consistent access is a business asset.

Sort found objects by three criteria before you commit: material compatibility (will it rust, melt, or react?), structural role (load-bearing or decorative?), and story value (can you name its origin for the buyer?). Story value is what allows a sculpture made from a bicycle chain and a maize grinder plate to sell for ten times its scrap weight.

3. Adhesives and Bonding Agents

Adhesives in mixed media do two jobs: bonding and sealing. Use them for the right job and they last decades; use them as a substitute for mechanical support and your sculpture will fail in the first hot season.

Table 2: Adhesive selection for metal mixed media
Adhesive Best for Working time Notes for African conditions
Two-part epoxy (steel-filled) Metalâstone, metalâmetal 10â40 min Best all-round; needs shade cure in high heat
Polyurethane construction adhesive Metalâwood 20â30 min Tolerates damp wood; expands â clamp firmly
Neutral-cure silicone Metalâglass 10â20 min skin Flexible; use acid-free, non-staining grade
Cyanoacrylate (superglue) Small decorative parts only Seconds Brittle in UV; never structural

Source: adhesive categories and cure behaviour based on 3M's industrial adhesives technical data (3m.com) and Loctite/Henkel design guidance for metal bonding (henkel-adhesives.com).

4. Mounting and Display Techniques

Mounting is where commissions are won or lost. A gallery buyer judges the base first. Practical rules:

  • Base weight: the base should be at least 25â30% of total sculpture weight for free-standing indoor work, and much heavier outdoors.
  • Three-point contact: never let a piece rest on two points; wind and vibration will tip it.
  • Reversible fixings: galleries and collectors prefer bolts and clips over permanent welds at the base, so the piece can be moved without damage.
  • Plinth interface: insert a neoprene or cork gasket between metal and plinth to stop scratching and galvanic staining.
  • Wall-mounted work: use a steel French cleat welded to the frame â cheap, strong, and easy to level.

5. Weatherproofing Outdoor Sculptures

Outdoor commissions are the biggest contracts available to African metal sculptors â hotels, municipalities, corporate campuses, memorials. They are also the fastest way to lose a reputation if the work stains or fails within one rainy season. The core principle: separate, drain, and coat.

  • Separate: isolate dissimilar metals with nylon washers or rubber gaskets to prevent galvanic corrosion.
  • Drain: drill 6â8 mm weep holes at the lowest point of any hollow section so water cannot pool inside the steel.
  • Coat: zinc-rich primer plus two topcoats of marine-grade enamel or polyurethane. In coastal cities (Mombasa, Durban, Lagos, Accra), add a third coat and re-coat every 18â24 months.
  • Wood outdoors: seal all end grain; use a UV-stable exterior oil, not varnish, in high-sun regions.
  • Stone outdoors: avoid soft soapstone in frost or heavy-rain zones; granite and laterite-based stone hold up better.

â  SAFETY WARNING â MIXED MEDIA WORKSHOP

  • Never weld, grind, or cut near wood dust, solvents, or glass. Wood dust is combustible; solvent vapour ignites. Keep a 10-metre separation between the hot-work zone and any combustible material, and store a dry-powder extinguisher within reach.
  • Glass: always wear cut-resistant gloves and safety glasses. Never handle broken glass with bare hands; use a dustpan and dispose in a rigid, labelled container.
  • Epoxy and polyurethane adhesives: skin sensitisation is permanent. Wear nitrile gloves and work in cross-ventilation. Do not use solvents to clean adhesive off skin â use the manufacturer's cleaner.
  • Stone dust (especially granite and soapstone): contains crystalline silica. Wet-cut or use a P2/N95 respirator. Dry sweeping is prohibited.
  • Galvanised metal: welding or heating releases toxic zinc fumes. Remove the coating by grinding in ventilated space, or weld outdoors with a respirator.

6. Project: Mixed Media Assemblage

Brief: design and build a 60â90 cm free-standing assemblage using at least three material families (steel + one of wood/glass/stone + one found object), suitable for outdoor display and sale.

Process: (1) sketch the silhouette and mark load paths; (2) build the steel core first and test balance with a dummy base; (3) drill all drain and fixing holes before assembly; (4) prime and paint the steel before attaching wood, glass, or stone; (5) bond non-metals with the correct adhesive from Table 2 and add a mechanical backup; (6) mount on a weighted base with isolating gaskets; (7) document the found-object story in a one-page certificate of origin â this is your pricing justification.

Costing target: keep material cost under 35% of your sale price. On a typical assemblage selling for the equivalent of USD 400â900 in a regional gallery, that leaves healthy margin for labour, transport, and re-coating.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Materials sorted and compatibility checked against Table 1 before any cutting.
  2. All dissimilar metals isolated with nylon, rubber, or neoprene.
  3. Weep holes drilled at the lowest point of every hollow section.
  4. Adhesive chosen by joint type (Table 2) and always backed by a mechanical fixing.
  5. Steel primed and top-coated before non-metal parts are attached.
  6. Base weight at least 25â30% of total sculpture weight; three-point contact minimum.
  7. Hot-work, glass, adhesive, and silica-dust controls in place before work starts.
  8. Found-object origin documented for the buyer; re-coating schedule agreed in writing for outdoor commissions.

Further Reading

  • Victoria and Albert Museum â Caring for your collection (mixed materials)
  • Canadian Conservation Institute â Agents of Deterioration
  • Engineering ToolBox â Coefficients of Linear Thermal Expansion
  • UK Health and Safety Executive â Crystalline silica dust controls
  • 3M â Bonding and Assembly technical resources

quiz.q: When combining metal with wood, why should you drill holes 2mm larger than the bolt diameter?
options: A) To allow for wood expansion and contraction
quiz.explanation: Wood moves with humidity, so oversized holes prevent cracking and joint failure.

quiz.q: Which adhesive is recommended for bonding glass to metal?
quiz.explanation: Silicone adhesive flexes with thermal expansion and adheres well to both glass and metal.

quiz.q: What is the best way to join stone to metal for an outdoor sculpture?
options: B) Use two-part epoxy and a mechanical support
quiz.explanation: Epoxy provides strong bonding, and a metal bracket supports the heavy stone.

quiz.q: Which type of wood is mentioned as suitable for combining with metal in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Mukwa, teak, and mahogany are hardwoods available in Africa that work well.

quiz.q: What should you do to glass before attaching it to metal to avoid sharp edges?
options: A) Tumble it with sand and water
quiz.explanation: Tumbling smooths sharp edges, making the glass safe to handle.

quiz.q: In found object sculpture, what is a good source of materials in Africa?
options: B) Juakali artisan clusters and scrapyards
quiz.explanation: Juakali clusters and scrapyards provide discarded metal and objects.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using hot glue for outdoor sculptures?
quiz.explanation: Hot glue softens and fails in high temperatures common in African sun.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to join found objects if you don't have a welder?
quiz.explanation: Bolts and rivets provide strong mechanical joints without welding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended cure time for epoxy at 25Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Most epoxies reach full strength after 24 hours at room temperature.

quiz.q: Which adhesive is best for metal-to-wood joints that need flexibility?
quiz.explanation: Polyurethane glue flexes with wood movement and bonds well to metal.

quiz.q: What is a key step before applying adhesive to metal?
options: B) Clean with acetone or alcohol
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes oil and dust, ensuring a strong bond.

quiz.q: Which material should you avoid for outdoor sculptures because it reacts with acid rain?
quiz.explanation: Limestone is soluble in acid rain, causing deterioration.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a French cleat in mounting?
options: A) To hang a sculpture on a wall
quiz.explanation: A French cleat is a beveled bracket system for secure wall mounting.

quiz.q: How deep should you dig a foundation hole for an outdoor sculpture?
quiz.explanation: A 30cm deep hole with concrete provides a stable base.

quiz.q: What is a good base material for a heavy indoor sculpture?
quiz.explanation: Wood or stone bases are heavy and stable, preventing tipping.

quiz.q: Why should you angle outdoor bases slightly?
options: B) To let water run off
D) To fit in a corner
quiz.explanation: Angling prevents water pooling, which can cause rust or rot.

quiz.q: What is a recommended primer for steel outdoors?
quiz.explanation: Zinc-rich primer provides rust protection for steel.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect an outdoor sculpture in a coastal area?
quiz.explanation: Salt accelerates corrosion, so monthly washing and inspection are needed.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to prevent water from collecting in hollow metal parts?
quiz.explanation: A 5mm drainage hole at the lowest point lets water escape.

quiz.q: Which finish is best for wood outdoors?
quiz.explanation: Marine varnish protects against moisture and UV.

quiz.q: What is the minimum height for the project sculpture?
quiz.explanation: The project requires a sculpture at least 40cm tall.

quiz.q: How many other materials besides metal must the project include?
quiz.explanation: The project must combine metal with at least two of wood, glass, or stone.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to protect wood when welding nearby?
options: A) Cover with a wet cloth
quiz.explanation: A wet cloth prevents wood from catching fire from sparks.

quiz.q: What should you do after completing your project?
options: B) Document with photos and description
quiz.explanation: Documentation helps you track your work and share it.

quiz.q: What is a recommended adhesive for metal-to-stone?
quiz.explanation: Two-part epoxy provides strong, durable bonding for stone and metal.

quiz.q: Why is surface preparation important for adhesive bonding?
options: A) It makes the adhesive dry faster
B) It removes oil and dust for better grip
quiz.explanation: Clean, roughened surfaces allow the adhesive to bond properly.

quiz.q: What is a good way to test a joint's strength?
options: B) Hit with a hammer hard
quiz.explanation: Gentle shaking reveals loose joints without damaging the sculpture.

quiz.q: Which of these is a found object commonly used in sculpture?
quiz.explanation: Bicycle chains are durable metal objects often used in assemblages.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ratio for concrete foundation mix?
quiz.explanation: A 1:2:3 mix by volume is standard for strong concrete.

quiz.q: What should you wear when grinding or welding?
quiz.explanation: A respirator protects from fumes, and safety glasses protect eyes from sparks.
